4c52bb5ce7762fca: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence.

Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks.
In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys.

“Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday.

Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama.
This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models.

In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks.

“The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote.

The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt.

In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.”

Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image.

While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote.
None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker.

“The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.”
The FBI weighs in

The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.”

The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants.
After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October.

However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI.

The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert.

These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

49b793be636601e9: After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads.

“Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial. “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.”

The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard, the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself).
A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine

Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects.
The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids.

Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it.

While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well).
The Web’s about to get lit
Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas.

Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example, the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls, can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js, or to create charts with D3.js.
Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon.
Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas, then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code.
HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X.

A trippy demo from html-in-canvas.dev shows a dragon slithering through the opening chapter of an online book, with the text smoothly reflowing in its wake. Try to shoo the beast off with your cursor and it will burn the virtual text with its fiery breath.
The source code reveals that “Margin Dragon” was rendered in 881 lines of vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code.
Another demo on the sample site is a “mouse-driven elastic displacement effect,” in which a “radial bulge” and drop shadow follow the cursor across the canvas.

Of course, such stylistic enchantments will not always be used for whimsy. Inevitably, unscrupulous marketers will discover powerful new ways to annoy us about all the virtues of late-stage capitalism.
“The world is not ready for HTML-in-Canvas,” a punter wrote on X.
Here be dragons

As per norm, HTML-in-Canvas has plenty of bugs (and it hasn’t even gone cross-platform yet). In some cases, the CSS doesn’t get painted on where it should, and timing with the reactive frameworks could be better synchronized.
And there is a lot for the lowly web maintainer to learn.

The core developers resolved the issue of canvas copying sensitive cross-origin data where it oughtn’t (as per CORS), but the API does not indicate when it declines to copy the data, leaving the community to file bug reports of what appear to be silent failures.
Likewise, developers must learn to properly document on-screen bounding boxes to keep accessibility tools like screen readers and click targets operating properly in 3D environments. ®

46cac4ef45279ad2: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind.

But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs, each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz.

The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer, built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking.

Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger.

ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs.

Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64.

As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. And if there is one thing LineShine does well, it’s scale.

In GPU-accelerated systems like El Cap, you’re lucky to push HPL to within 70 percent of the system’s theoretical roofline. But LineShine isn’t GPU-accelerated. Sure, with 16 HBM stacks, the LX2 looks a lot like a GPU, but it's really just an enormous CPU with enough vector and matrix units to put more than a few modern GPUs to shame.
With enough of them – by which we mean 22,680 dual-socket nodes – NSCS catapulted China to the top of the Top500 for the first time in nearly a decade.
Not the benchmark it used to be
The US has no shortage of systems capable of eclipsing El Capitan or even LineShine’s performance if someone were motivated enough to get HPL running on them.

SpaceXAI’s 300 megawatt Colossus supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, boasts 200,000 Hopper GPUs each good for 34-67 (vector/matrix) teraFLOPS of FP64 grunt. Even assuming an abysmal 25% efficiency, the cluster should be more than capable of breaking three exaFLOPs in HPL.

It might need 10x the power of El Capitan, but the thing is, beyond winning points with the White House — a ship that has almost certainly sailed for Elon Musk after the DOGE fiasco — renting out the cluster to Anthropic to train and run Claude is a far more lucrative endeavor.
The same could be said of any number of AI clusters, from Meta’s Prometheus to OpenAI’s Starship.
It used to be that the systems to summit the Top500 were among the largest computers humanity has ever built. But this hasn’t been true in some time.
The US is starving for compute. HPL or even its sibling High-Performance Gradient Conjugate just aren’t the benchmarks to beat any longer.
The new battleground isn’t nuclear proliferation; it’s one of AI models, agents, and the means to harness them.

We’re not talking about tokens, LLMs, or chatbots, but the ability to harness these models to automate laboratories and formulate and test hypotheses long after the scientists they serve have gone home for dinner.
It’s why the US’s Genesis mission puts such a strong emphasis on AI.

AI-driven labs present an opportunity for researchers to iterate faster. Rather than running hundreds or thousands or simulations trying to find a needle in a haystack, a task for which a bigger iron is warranted, AI analysis and automation could focus that search.

High-performance computing (HPC), and by extension the Top500, will remain relevant as long as more FLOPS means more simulations per unit of time. But these systems can only move as fast as the men and women who operate them. ®

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?
3ec3fbaaa5e4180c: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime.
NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way.
“Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.”

Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either.

According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place.
“We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present.

AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised.
The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA.
But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example.
Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends.

“Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years.
The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said.

We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

ff0169702f8be68d: The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it.

Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine.

The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it.

Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs.

Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it.

Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes.
Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx.

Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready.

His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server.

In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service.

A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5.
For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue.

Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces.

Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®

b2955c38ff71d9a1: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.
Where traditional definitions of trust fall short

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.
Building trust that scales

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:
What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution.
Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds.

Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step.
Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows.
Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle.

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

9af9c51a7fd2f67a: From Abd Rahim Romle and Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim

A Malaysian applying for a licence, renewing a permit, or seeking government assistance should not have to navigate several websites, remember multiple passwords, or repeatedly submit the same information. Yet for some, accessing public services can still feel more complicated than it should.
We have become good at introducing digital platforms. The more important question is whether these platforms are making life easier for the rakyat.

Malaysia's digital transformation has brought improvements to public administration. Online apps, electronic payments, and digital records have reduced the need for physical visits and made many services more convenient.
These achievements deserve recognition. However, digital progress should not be measured simply by the number of apps launched or systems developed.
A government service is only successful when people can use it easily, reliably, and without unnecessary frustration.

Consider a small business owner applying for an operating licence. The application may be available online, but if the process still requires repeated document submissions, unclear approvals, or visits to different departments, digitalisation has merely changed the location of the bureaucracy.
The same applies to a parent seeking educational assistance, or an elderly person accessing healthcare services.
For these Malaysians, convenience matters more than the technology behind the system.

The 13th Malaysia Plan (2026-2030) places digital transformation and public service efficiency among Malaysia's development priorities. The challenge is ensuring that these ambitions translate into improvements that citizens can experience.

One persistent concern is fragmentation. Different agencies may operate separate systems with different registration requirements, procedures and user interfaces. While each platform may serve an administrative purpose, the combined experience can become confusing.
Citizens should not have to understand the organisational structure of government simply to obtain a service.

A more effective approach would focus on integrating services around people's needs. For example, starting a small business involves several administrative requirements. Instead of expecting entrepreneurs to navigate multiple agencies independently, government systems should provide clearer guidance and better coordination.
Similarly, families applying for assistance should not repeatedly provide information already held by public institutions, subject to appropriate privacy safeguards.

Another challenge is digital inclusion. Not every Malaysian has reliable internet access, the latest smartphone, or sufficient digital literacy to navigate complicated applications. Older citizens, rural communities, and people with disabilities may face additional difficulties.
Digital transformation should, therefore, preserve accessible alternatives while improving online services.

Three priorities deserve attention. First, government agencies should evaluate digital platforms through citizen experience rather than technological output. Processing times, successful applications, accessibility, and complaint resolution should become central performance indicators.

Second, greater emphasis should be placed on interoperability and administrative simplification. Agencies must improve information-sharing and eliminate unnecessary procedures before transferring them online.

Third, public servants should receive continuous training to provide responsive assistance across both digital and physical service channels. Technology cannot compensate for unclear procedures, weak coordination, or poor communication.

Importantly, public feedback must play a stronger role in evaluating service quality. When citizens report difficulties, their experiences should inform system improvements rather than disappear into administrative complaint channels.

Malaysia does not necessarily need another app whenever a service problem emerges. Sometimes, improving an existing platform, simplifying a form, or ensuring that someone answers a telephone call would make a greater difference. The objective should never be digitalisation for its own sake.

Malaysia's ambition to become a competitive digital economy depends partly on building public institutions that are efficient, trustworthy and responsive. A well-designed digital government should save citizens time, reduce costs, and make essential services easier to access.

The rakyat do not judge government efficiency by how many digital platforms exist. They judge it by whether applications are processed promptly, information is clear, and problems are resolved without unnecessary obstacles.
Malaysia's next public sector breakthrough may not require another digital platform. It may simply require making the services we already have work better for everyone.

Abd Rahim Romle is an associate professor and deputy dean at the Ghazali Shafie Graduate School of Government at Universiti Utara Malaysia. Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim is a Master of Teaching English as a Second Language candidate at Universiti Putra Malaysia.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.
“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.
Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to SoundCloud, where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she uploaded it to YouTube and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video. Unbeknownst to Shokin, her version of “Bre Petruinko” had become popular among DJs and electronic artists and had been sampled in dozens of songs. Someone in the comments pointed her towards one of the more popular tracks. “I look up this video and it’s something that has millions of hits [...] and 30 seconds into this track I hear my own voice and I was utterly shocked. I didn’t know how to react,” she said (the video has more than 4 million views).

“The first thing that comes to mind is, ‘Oh my god, someone stole my voice and didn’t credit me,’” she said. Shokin said she talked to a lot of DJs and figured out how they’d gotten her voice. They’d purchased a pack of samples from a company called Loopmasters that was selling her version of “Bre Petruinko” as part of its “Folk Legends” set.

“I got in touch with the distributor and they were deeply apologetic. They were unaware that this had happened and they immediately tried to make right of the situation and granted me royalties on the sample pack,” Shokin said. “At that point, countless DJs and music producers had been using my voice for their own tracks, unbeknownst to me. At least I’m aware and at least I was making something off of it and I was satisfied with that. I didn’t love the way that it came about, but whatever, they tried to make right of the situation.”

But Shokin’s “Bre Petruinko” saga wasn’t over. Last month, she opened YouTube and noticed her original recording was gone. A company called Media Nov Records had issued a copyright strike against her song, and YouTube had taken it down.She thought it would be easy to get this reversed. It’s a public domain folk song and she had the original recordings and a history with a distributor. “If I just explain it to YouTube, they’ll understand,” she thought.

Media Nov Records advertises itself as a “distribution company” that that partners with artists to release their music on digital platforms. But a lot of its website focuses on rights management and copyright protection. “At Media Nov, we go above and beyond to safeguard your musical creations. Our comprehensive rights management system leverages cutting-edge technology and legal expertise to ensure you receive the royalties you deserve,” it said on its website.

YouTube uses automated systems to work through copyright claims. When someone files a claim against a video, the company tends to automatically approve it. The original uploader can file a “counterclaim,” where they argue that the video should stay up, or that it should not be demonetized.

Shokin filed two counterclaims, but neither worked. “It's unclear to us whether you have a valid reason for filing a counter notification, so we won't be able to honor your request,” YouTube said in its last denial. It told her to contact the copyright holder; in this case, it was a public domain song and so there was no actual “copyright holder,” just Media Nov, which was claiming to hold it.

“I tried emailing them,” she said. “I tried calling them. There doesn’t appear to be a working phone line. I got in touch with [Loopmaster, which was selling her recording]. They tried getting in touch. I’m being ignored by everybody, by YouTube, by this media company that, like, the website seems to be entirely AI-generated, and all I want is to talk to a human about this.”

Media Nov’s site boasted about its use of automated DMCA takedowns, YouTube content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition. “Our advanced AI identifies your music across platforms ensuring accurate tracking and protection,” it said. The company says it has been in existence since 1996, but Archive.org’s Wayback Machine doesn’t show much of a web presence until last year. Its website is basic and barebones.

The company has two addresses on its website. One is an apartment building in Los Angeles on Marina Del Rey. The other is the Black Church in Dublin, Ireland — a cathedral that’s been converted into an office space. The site listed a Los Angeles phone number that was busy every time 404 Media tried to call it.

According to corporate paperwork filed in Ireland and reviewed by 404 Media, Media Nov Records was founded a little more than a year ago. Its listed address is the Black Church in Ireland but both of its shareholders gave addresses in Turkey.

404 Media found four different YouTube pages managed by Media Nov Records. Each contained hundreds of videos — many with AI-generated art assets and music. The songs are sometimes cross posted between the different channels and are mostly looping electronic beats. Think low effort “lofi beats” knock offs. The art assets are footage of sports cars, anime girls, and AI-generated pictures of women. The songs are cross posted on multiple channels and often generate fewer than 100 views. Each also has few YouTube shorts that revolve around “random acts of kindness.” A Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok) watermark is present in some of these videos.

For example, recent YouTube shorts on its flagship page include a basic beat playing over an AI-generated woman mopping the floor of a store while being berated by her AI-generated boss. Another features an AI-generated woman crying over a well, and a crew of men rescuing her child. One of its other pages looks like this:

Media Nov Records told 404 Media that it operates 500 of these channels and “works with various artists, content creators, and music partners.” The company did not initially return emails or phone calls from Shokin or Loopmaster, but responded to an email from 404 Media.

It said it would look into its copyright claim of Shokin’s track. “We remain willing to review the relevant ownership documentation, original audio files, and supporting evidence to investigate the copyright claim thoroughly. If an error is identified, we are committed to taking appropriate corrective action promptly,” it said.

After 404 Media requested comment, Media Nov Records responded to Shokin and asked her to provide “relevant documentation supporting her ownership of the recording, including original audio files, recording evidence, original publication dates, and any other supporting materials,” which is a wild request considering that it has nothing to do with her recording and does not own the copyright.

The company told 404 Media that Shokin and Loopmaster’s emails had gone to its spam folder. “Regarding ‘Bre Petrunko,’ we would like to clarify that the musical composition and arrangement rights associated with Philip Koutev’s work must be distinguished from the rights in any individual sound recording. Media Nov Records also holds certain rights relating to the relevant musical content,” the company told Shokin in an email reviewed by 404 Media.

“Bre Petrunko” is an old folk song with no known writer. It’s primarily sung and most performances of it do not use instruments. Philip Koutev is a Bulgarian composer who popularized a version of the song in 1963. He died in 1982 and the copyright for that particular version is held by the Smithsonian. There are also many other versions of the song on YouTube, some with millions of views.

“Recording your own cover or performance does not automatically establish ownership of the underlying composition or arrangement. Likewise, rights in the underlying musical work do not automatically establish ownership of your particular recording,” Media Nov said.

“It’s ironic that they’re in the copyright business,” Shokin said. “It’s not the arrangement that’s in question. It’s the voice and performance [...] they clearly have no clue what they’re talking about.”

It's unclear why Media Nov Records brought Koutev into the conversation. 404 Media asked which song or work in its catalog triggered the copyright notice against Shokin but Media Nov Records did not respond.

“That makes it really ridiculous,” Alfred Steiner, an artist and copyright lawyer, told 404 Media. “If it’s her voice and her playing instruments, what could she possibly be infringing if it’s a folk song from the 19th century?”

The situation between Shokin and Media Nov Records sounded odd to Steiner. “I've seen lots of providers where you say ‘I have the rights’ and basically say nothing more than that, and they put it back because they’re taking a risk now. They’re harming her. If they just put it back, they’re at no risk,” he said.

“It sounds, to me, like a small company — despite the fact that they represent or run 500 YouTube channels — that are understaffed and is using a lot of different tools, probably a lot of AI, to identify tracks that are ostensibly owned by its clients and then automatically filing takedown requests,” he said. “They’re probably taking down far more than they have the right to take down.”

Minutes after it sent Shokin an email asking for proof she’d recorded the song, Media Nov Records followed up in an email addressed to both 404 Media and Shokin. “Following our review, Media Nov Records has decided to retract the copyright removal request for Samantha Shokin’s video. We are taking this step because the video has not generated revenue or received views, and we do not consider maintaining the removal request necessary at this stage,” it said. “However, this decision does not constitute a waiver of any rights we may hold. We intend to initiate appropriate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute.”
Around 24 hours later, Shokin’s original video was back up. A spokesperson for YouTube confirmed that it reinstated the video after the claimant withdrew their complaint.
“It sounds like they got scared and feel like this is not a battle worth fighting,” Shokin said after seeing the email from Media Nov Records.

“Submitting a takedown request for rights that you don’t have can subject you to liability which includes actual damages and costs and attorney’s fees,” Steiner told 404 Media. “Doing this on a slipshod, shotgun approach is inadvisable from my perspective. Of course, if all of the people you end up offending are small parties and don’t have the resources to respond through the court system, and you are a fly-by-night entity that is hard to pin down and nobody knows who you are [...] it can be difficult to get a remedy.”

Shokin said she felt vindicated but was unhappy that it took a journalist emailing Media Nov Records to get them to listen to her. “They got my emails and they got Loopmaster’s email and they were just ignoring it because they only decided to respond because they got scared that it’ll be bad press,” she said. “It’s just not great all around. The whole system is broken. It feels like a broken system.”

6368ac2908033cb4: SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.

While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.

“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.
12604af31481c12b: Butterball Turkey Talk-Line experts take part in cooking and carving classes in 2009. AP Photo/M. Spencer GreenOne of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm, Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays. I find turkeys fascinating, because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business. More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg). While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway. Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies, researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving. Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound, while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched. Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken. So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans. And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn. The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds. Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken. In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week. Raymond Baker carves a turkey in 1948 while his wife and 16 kids surround him. Getty Images There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours, while a 4-pound chicken takes about two. That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society. In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut. He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one. They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take. I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket. Jay L. Zagorsky does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
36ae6e814e5b9164: The transcript from this week’s, MiB: Vanguard CEO Salim Ramji, is below.

Masters in Business: Salim Ramji, CEO of Vanguard Interview transcript · Bloomberg Radio
[00:00:02] Bloomberg Audio Studios, podcasts, radio, news.

[00:00:07] BARRY RITHOLTZ: This week on the podcast, yet another fascinating conversation. I sit down with Vanguard’s CEO, Salim Ramji. Previously he was at BlackRock, helping to oversee iShares and indexing. He’s got a fascinating background, and really is one of the people in the wealth management industry who is so uniquely situated to see all of these different things that are going on.

What a great perch to observe the future of wealth management. I thought this conversation was fascinating, and I think you will also. With no further ado, my conversation with Vanguard’s Salim Ramji. Salim, welcome to Bloomberg.
[00:00:58] SALIM RAMJI: Well, thanks, Barry. It’s great to be back. I think we did this about half a dozen years ago, right?
[00:01:02] BARRY RITHOLTZ: In the middle of peak COVID. It was a frightening time.
[00:01:07] SALIM RAMJI: It’s nice to be in a studio.
[00:01:09] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yes. I want to talk about your career and what led you to Vanguard. But I have to start by asking about your academic background.
Bachelor’s in economics and politics from the University of Toronto, and then a master’s in law at Cambridge. And I’m assuming a master’s at Cambridge is like a JD here, is that right?
[00:01:19] SALIM RAMJI: Yeah, kind of.
[00:01:33] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Was the original career plan becoming an attorney?

[00:01:37] SALIM RAMJI: Neither of my parents finished high school. My dad used to run a grocery store that I worked in as a kid. And from my parents’ point of view, they just wanted me to go to college. I don’t think there was any great original plan other than I thought going to college would be a good thing. I was drawn to the law, and ultimately my first job was at a law firm in London, in part because there were so many exciting and interesting things happening in the world of law and business in the early nineties in Europe at the time.

And so that, for me, was a compelling piece. But I wasn’t one of these kids who, from the age of 10, wanted to be a lawyer. It was more—it felt like a really interesting time, with markets liberalizing and lots of new markets opening up all over the world.

[00:02:41] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m curious how your upbringing affected how you look at money. You mentioned you worked in your dad’s grocery store; both your parents were immigrants working and living in British Columbia. How did that affect your relationship with money and work?

[00:02:56] SALIM RAMJI: It probably—some of these things you don’t really truly understand until years later. But we didn’t always have a lot of financial security growing up. And I’m at a company that cares very deeply about people’s financial security, and you can sometimes abstract that away in terms of what it means.

But at least for me, I know what having it is, and I know what the absence of it is. Obviously, having some financial security is far better. And I think it really drove home for me the real importance, at a very personal level, of what financial security means in somebody’s life or somebody’s family, and the importance of it to so many other things: the general happiness of the house, the levels of stress in the house, the freedom to be able to do things once you’ve attained it. And so financial security is something that I know deeply, because I know its absence too.
And so I think it makes it meaningful for me. Even if you asked the 20-year-old version of me, I wouldn’t have thought of it in that way.

[00:04:12] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I think a lot of people don’t realize the first checkbox—lack of financial stress—is a huge weight off people’s minds. So if you could solve for that, everything after that feels like gravy.
[00:04:23] SALIM RAMJI: Yeah. No, I absolutely agree.
[00:04:26] BARRY RITHOLTZ: So you’re working in London at Clifford Chance, and you also spent some time in Hong Kong? Was that doing legal work, or was that—
[00:04:33] SALIM RAMJI: I did. It was doing legal work.
[00:04:34] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And then how do you transition from that to McKinsey? What led to that?

[00:04:39] SALIM RAMJI: I enjoyed the business part of being a lawyer. I’d worked in financial markets, in M&A, and I was always interested in what happened after the deal closed, in the business aspects. And McKinsey offered me the chance to still be in a professional services firm, which I liked, still serve clients, which I liked, but also to get a little deeper on the business of things. And I had a wonderful career there for a dozen or so years, really learning about financial institutions and advising a whole range of financial institutions in New York and beyond.

[00:05:23] BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m fascinated, ’cause attorneys and consultants advise people running businesses, and then you made the transition to actually running a business at BlackRock. And when you were at McKinsey, you were running their asset and wealth management practice, so it wasn’t a radical jump to go to BlackRock, but how different is it offering advice versus actually, where the rubber meets the road, actually running the shop?

[00:05:50] SALIM RAMJI: It’s really different. And I’d worked with them as a client for a number of years before joining them. It’s a very different aspect when you’re owning the outcomes, when you’re having to lead broader groups of people.

And when you’re having to sweat every single detail, every single moment of every single day. And it was a great learning experience for me, ’cause I joined them in my early forties, and it’s a chance to really learn a whole new set of skills. Even though you know the industry, and you think you know a thing or two about the firm, you really don’t until you’re deep into it.
And for me it was a great source of renewal, revitalization, a whole series of things that, even to this day, I’m very grateful for.

[00:06:47] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And I think—if my research is correct—you started in 2014 at BlackRock as head of corporate strategy, which is probably the most advice-oriented position within BlackRock. You’re advising the board, you’re advising management: hey, this is our strategic outlook, here’s how we should proceed.

From there you end up running US Wealth Advisory and eventually taking over iShares and index investing in 2019, which I want to say was about $3 trillion, more or less. I don’t know if it started there or finished there, but about that. That’s some real money. Now you’re actually running a business, as opposed to offering advice, at BlackRock. Tell us what it was like taking over such a massive part of the firm.
[00:07:40] SALIM RAMJI: You’re talking about—
[00:07:42] BARRY RITHOLTZ: iShares. iShares and index investing.

[00:07:44] SALIM RAMJI: It was a bit of a journey. I probably spent about a year in corporate strategy, and that was really—I got to learn the culture of the firm. I got to learn the people at the firm. I can’t say I had a tremendous impact in that year, but it really led to the business of serving a whole range of financial advisors all across the United States.

And that for me was fascinating, because I got to spend time with financial advisors in every major city, several not-so-major cities all across the US, and understand how they were looking to grow their practices, grow their businesses. Many of them were effectively mid-size business owners. And the chance to really understand what their needs were, how they served their clients, was really meaningful.
And for iShares it was just really expanding that on a much more global scale, given the global breadth of that firm.

[00:08:48] BARRY RITHOLTZ: So iShares has become legendary. It’s probably the single most successful M&A action taken by any asset manager, and has just grown into one of the most important parts of the world of advisory. When you assume a leadership role at a division like that, that’s so important and has been running on all cylinders for so long, is there any reluctance to interfere with what’s working?

On the one hand, you can’t just rely on its momentum, ’cause eventually that peters out. How do you figure out, hey, we want to step on the accelerator without killing the goose—to mix metaphors—that laid the golden egg?

[00:09:38] SALIM RAMJI: Well, the thing about any markets business is that the momentum sometimes interrupts you. And so you don’t have a great choice in terms of how things evolve. And when we last spoke six years ago, right in the throes of COVID and the pandemic, a few months before there were also big dislocations happening in the bond market. And so one of the things that I learned was just about how to maintain the resiliency of investments that millions of people rely on, particularly in moments of stress. And some of that translates through to Vanguard today.

’Cause even at moments that look like they’re not gonna have big disruptions, that doesn’t mean they might not a few months from now or a few years from now. And the thing about investments, and particularly things like index investments or ETFs, people naturally expect them to work not just some of the time, but all of the time. And that’s an inherent part of the operation of it. But there’s a whole range of underlying pieces, whether it’s in how our portfolio managers manage the assets, or in how the system of broker-dealers and exchange providers and index providers helps maintain an orderly system.

But one of the things that really struck home to me, back in 2019 and especially in 2020, was you can’t take any of that for granted. And that requires work every single moment of every single day to make sure all the investments work as they ought to.

[00:11:25] BARRY RITHOLTZ: It’s kind of funny, because we had been warned, hey, just wait for the next dislocation: indexing’s gonna fail, ETFs are gonna fail. And it turned out, especially down 34% in about six weeks in the first quarter of 2020, indexing and ETFs both held up.
What do you attribute that to?

[00:11:45] SALIM RAMJI: Well, one of the books I’ve been reading was by a guest you just had on the show, Robin’s book about fabulous debt and the bond markets. And with each of the dislocations—and let me go back to the dislocation in 2020—I thought the most interesting set of things that happened back then was what happened in the bond market. The bond market was dislocated. The ETF market was not.

And what really catalyzed that dislocation was a whole series of movements towards ETFs, towards electronic venues, towards more exchange-traded versus over-the-counter pieces. And the bond market, even today, six years later, is still in need of modernization. But that was a real catalyst to help the bond market modernize. If you go back even earlier to the financial crisis, markets dislocated, but more and more investors moved into index investing and particularly ETF investing.

And we saw that in Vanguard’s flows at the time. And each dislocation results in learnings about the market structure. And at least in more recent history, it’s made market structure better, because consumers and investors learn a few things.

And it’s how do you make sure that the system remains resilient through each one of these. But I think ETFs, whether it’s bond ETFs or equity ETFs, even if I look back over the past 15 years, have weathered most or almost everything that’s been thrown at them.
[00:13:27] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I have so many questions for you about running Vanguard and the future of that company. But last question before we get to that.
You worked very closely with Larry Fink. How did his leadership affect how you think about running a company? What did you take from him?

[00:13:48] SALIM RAMJI: I did, for nearly a dozen years. Well, founders are different, right? Founders—and you’ll know this too, given your role at Ritholtz—but founders are different than CEOs. And I think the thing I really learned from that whole experience was the need to always be able to reinvent and look around corners and anticipate a series of things. And I think learning from the founder of a company that’s built the company up at scale was a really great way, in my broad business experience, to learn something new and learn it from someone who started the firm.

[00:14:29] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really, really interesting. Coming up, we continue our conversation with Salim Ramji, CEO of Vanguard, discussing what it takes to run one of the largest asset managers in the world. I’m Barry Ritholtz. You are listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio.
I’m Barry Ritholtz. You are listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio.
My extra special guest today is Salim Ramji. He is CEO of the Vanguard Group, helping to oversee about $12.5 trillion. Is that about right?
[00:14:52] SALIM RAMJI: About right, in client assets.

[00:15:05] BARRY RITHOLTZ: By the time this airs it’ll be 13 and change. So I have been fortunate enough to have interviewed every Vanguard CEO back to Jack Bogle. And now that you are here, I’m actually interviewing you as CEO. You are the first outsider to run Vanguard, which is kind of fascinating. And you never worked directly with Jack Bogle.
So the first question I have to ask about operations at Vanguard is, how do you win the trust of the crew as an outsider?

[00:15:40] SALIM RAMJI: Yeah, it’s a great question. It was just under three years ago—I guess it was May 2024—and the board had appointed me, but I was now meeting the crew for the first time. And the thing about Vanguard, and I’d always seen this from the outside, about the culture and the mission orientation: Vanguard’s always had that in its reputation.

It’s hard to explain, Barry, but from the inside, just how real that is. And whether I go back to May 2024 and just really seeing it and feeling it—I almost felt like—there’s that David Foster Wallace speech that he gave at Kenyon College, “This Is Water,” right? The big fish goes up to two small fishes and asks them, “How’s the water?” And one of the small fishes asks, “What the hell is water?”

Right? And for us, our culture was so real and so unusual. It’s quite unlike any other company I’ve worked at or even advised earlier in my career. And I think the extraordinary thing about it is that it’s been several years now since Bogle passed.

I’m the fifth CEO since him. The company’s a lot bigger than it was 10 years ago or 25 years ago, but the culture is very real. And so I spent a lot of time in my first year meeting crew members at our different sites across the United States and outside the United States, understanding what it is about the culture that made it so pervasive and so real, even at our scale. And giving them an opportunity to ask me a bunch of questions, which were really: do I believe in the mission, in the culture, and in the values of the company?

I probably met more people in my first six or nine months at Vanguard than I’d met in my entire life beforehand. But a lot of it was just around me coming to appreciate what went into building that, and for the crew to understand what made me excited and what made me tick. And starting to connect both of those things in terms of how do we preserve and maintain the mission and the culture while being able to develop and do a whole new set of things strategically.

11cf973c0d595b96: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”

That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says.

Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.
